column2: I am different from the seer, hearer, speaker, doer and enjoyer; I am the Self of knowledge, eternal, continuous, actionless, limitless, unattached and full.
I am not this, nor that; I am the supreme, pure illuminator of both, empty of outside and inside — the full, non-dual Brahman.
The incomparable, beginningless reality, far from the imagining "you, I, this, that," of one taste of eternal bliss, the truth — Brahman, non-dual, am I.

I am Narayana, I am the destroyer of Naraka, I am the destroyer of the (three) cities; I am the Person, I am the Lord. I am undivided knowledge, the witness of all; I have no Lord over me, no ego and no possessiveness.
I alone abide in all beings, as the Self of knowledge, the support within and without; I am the enjoyer and the enjoyed, myself all — whatever was seen before as separate "this."
In me, the ocean of undivided bliss, the waves of the universe arise and dissolve in many ways, through the play of the wind of Maya.

Gross and other states are imagined in me through delusion, and are superimposed by people who perceive them, as, in time, the seasons, half-years, years and ages are imagined in the partless and free of alternatives.
What is superimposed never harms its substratum, though the deluded are affected by great faults; the great flood of a mirage does not moisten even a patch of barren ground.
I am far from being tainted, like space; I am different from what is illumined, like the sun; I am always unmoving, like a mountain; I am without a shore, like the ocean.
I have no connection with the body, as the sky has none with a cloud; so how can the states of waking, dream and deep sleep, which are its properties, be mine?
The adjunct comes and goes; it alone acts and enjoys; it alone decays and dies. I always stay unmoving like a great mountain.
I have neither engagement nor withdrawal, being always of one form and without parts. How can that which is one Self, dense, continuous, full like space, exert itself?
How can merit and sin belong to me, who am without senses, without mind, without change and without form, the experience of undivided bliss? Scripture says, "It is not followed by (good and evil)."
Whatever heat or cold, good or bad, touches the shadow does not touch the person at all, who is different from it.
The properties of what is witnessed do not touch the witness, who is distinct; like the properties of a house to the lamp that lights it, the properties of body, senses and mind never touch the Self.
As the sun is the witness of actions, as fire has the power to burn (iron), and as a rope has connection with what is superimposed on it, so too is it with me, the unchanging Self of consciousness.
I am neither doer nor causer of action; neither enjoyer nor causer of enjoyment; neither seer nor causer of seeing. I am that self-luminous, incomparable Self.
When the adjunct moves, the deluded attribute the trembling of the reflection to the original, like the sun, which is actionless: "I am the doer, I am the enjoyer, alas, I am killed!"
Whether in water or on land, let this inert (body) roll about; I am not touched by its properties, as space by the properties of a pot.

Agency, enjoyment, wickedness, intoxication, dullness, bondage, liberation and the like are alternatives of the intellect; in truth they do not exist in the Supreme Brahman, alone, non-dual, one's own Self.
Let the modifications of Nature be ten, a hundred, or a thousand; what are they to me, the unattached consciousness? Does a cloud ever touch the sky?
That in which this universe, from the Unmanifest to the gross, is perceived as a mere appearance, which is like space, subtle, without beginning or end — non-dual Brahman — that I am.
The support of all, the illuminator of all things, having all forms, all-pervading, empty of everything, eternal, pure, unmoving, free of alternatives — non-dual Brahman — that I am.
In which all special features of Maya have been set aside, the inner reality, not reached by perceptions, truth, knowledge, infinite, of the form of bliss — non-dual Brahman — that I am.
I am actionless, I am unchanging, I am without parts, I am formless; I am free of alternatives, I am eternal, I am without support, I am without a second.
I am the Self of all, I am all, I am beyond all, I am non-dual; I am alone, undivided knowledge, I am bliss, unbroken.
This glory of the empire of self-rule has been gained by me through the grace of your glorious greatness. To you, great-souled revered teacher, homage, homage, and again homage.

In the great dream, wandering in the forest of birth, old age and death made by Maya, daily tormented by heavy afflictions, and distressed by the tiger of egoism, you, O teacher, out of great compassion have awakened me from sleep and protected me.

Homage to that One, ever one, to some (indescribable) radiance; homage again and again to the one radiance of consciousness, which shines forth in the form of this universe — O king of teachers, yours.

Thus seeing the excellent disciple bowing, who had reached the happiness of the Self and awakened to the truth, the great-souled lord of teachers, with a delighted heart, spoke again this excellent word.

Therefore the world is a continuous stream of the thought of Brahman; see everything as Brahman alone, with the eye of the Self and a tranquil mind, in all states. What else is seen by people with eyes than form? So for the knower of Brahman, what else is there as a field for the mind's play?
Who, having tasted that experience of the taste of supreme bliss, would delight in empty things? When the moon, greatly delightful, is shining, who would wish to look at a painted moon?

By experiencing unreal things there is no contentment and no removal of sorrow; therefore, contented with the experience of the taste of non-dual bliss, remain happily in steadfastness in the real Self.
Seeing only yourself in every way, thinking of yourself as non-dual, enjoying your own bliss everywhere — pass your time, O great-minded one.

Imagining alternatives in the Self of undivided knowledge, free of alternatives, is like imagining a city in the sky; therefore, always in the non-dual form of bliss, having attained supreme peace, practise silence.

The state of silence is supreme calm, of the intellect that is the cause of imagined alternatives of the unreal; for the great soul, the knower of Brahman, the Self of Brahman, in whom is the bliss of non-dual happiness, unbroken.
There is no higher happiness-giving state than silence free of habit-impressions, for one who has known the nature of the Self and drinks the taste of his own bliss.
Walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or in any other way, let the wise man live as he pleases, ever the sage delighting in the Self.

For the great soul who has perfected the truth, whose mind's activity is not bound by place, time, posture, direction, restraint and the like, or by a target and so on — what rule or condition is there for the knowledge of himself?
For knowing 'this is a pot,' what rule is required? Only the soundness of the means of knowledge is needed, when it exists the perception of the thing arises.
This Self, eternally established, is revealed when the means of knowledge exists; it requires no place, no time, no purification.
The knowledge 'I am Devadatta' is independent of anything; so too is this knowledge 'I am Brahman' of the knower of Brahman.
By whose light all this world shines, as by the sun — what could illumine that (Self), when the not-Self is unreal and worthless?
The Vedas, the scriptures, the Puranas and all beings are meaningful through Him; what could illumine that knower?
This self-luminous Self of infinite power, immeasurable, the experience of all — knowing whom alone one is freed from bondage — this best of the knowers of Brahman is victorious.
He is neither distressed nor delighted by objects, neither attached nor averse; he plays always in himself, rejoicing, satisfied with the taste of unbroken bliss.
As a child forgets hunger and bodily pain and plays with a toy, so the wise man, free of possessiveness and ego, is happy and delights (in the Self).

Free from worry, alms without humiliation as food, water from rivers to drink, an unhindered life in independence, fearless sleep in a cemetery or forest, clothes needing no washing or drying, the quarters for dress, the earth for bed, wandering along the paths of the Vedanta — the play of the knowers in the Supreme Brahman.
Using this body as a vehicle, he enjoys all the objects that come, at the will of others, like a child — the knower of the Self, whose marks are hidden and whose outward life is unattached.
Whether naked or clothed, or wearing skin, or dwelling in the garment of consciousness, he moves on the earth like a madman, or like a child, or like a ghoul.
The sage wanders alone, without desire though seeming to desire; always contented in himself, himself established as the Self of all.

Sometimes a fool, sometimes a sage, sometimes with the splendour of a great king, sometimes wandering, sometimes gentle, sometimes behaving like a python, sometimes honoured, sometimes despised, sometimes unknown — thus the wise man moves, ever happy with supreme bliss.
Though without wealth, always contented; though without help, very strong; though not eating, always satisfied; though without equal, seeing all alike.
Though acting, not acting; though enjoying fruits, not an enjoyer; though embodied, bodiless; though limited, all-pervading.
Neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant, neither the good nor the evil, ever touches this knower of Brahman, who is always without a body.

For the proud one who is connected with the gross body and the like, there are happiness and sorrow, good and evil; but for the sage whose bonds are destroyed, the real Self, whence good or evil, or their fruit?
As the sun, though not swallowed, is said by people to be swallowed (in an eclipse) through delusion, being ignorant of the nature of the thing —
so the fools, seeing the appearance of a body, through delusion see the best of the knowers of Brahman, though free of the bonds of body and the like, as if embodied.
A snake, having cast off its sloughed skin, stays apart from it, moved here and there by the wind; (so the knower's body is moved by the breath).
As a log is carried by the current to low or high ground, so the body is carried by fate to its enjoyments, at the proper times.

With the habit-impressions shaped by prarabdha karma, the one whose body is free acts in enjoyments like a worldly person; the perfected one himself dwells here as a witness, silent, like the hub of a wheel, free of alternatives and imaginings.

He neither directs the senses to objects nor withdraws them, standing as a mere spectator; nor does he look even slightly for the fruit of action, his mind intoxicated with drinking the thick taste of his own bliss.
He who, giving up the path of the seen and the unseen, stays as the Self alone — that best of the knowers of Brahman is himself directly Shiva.
The best of the knowers of Brahman is always liberated even while living, his purpose fulfilled; on the destruction of the adjunct, being Brahman, he merges into the non-dual Brahman.
As an actor is the same whether he has his costume on or off, so the best of the knowers of Brahman is always Brahman alone, nothing else.
Wherever this body falls, like a withered leaf of a tree, for the ascetic who has become Brahman, it was burned before by the fire of consciousness.
For the sage established in the real Self, Brahman, always in the nature of full, non-dual bliss, there is no waiting for a suitable place or time for laying down this heap of skin, flesh and filth.
The release of the body is not liberation, nor is that of the staff and water-pot; the release of the knot of ignorance in the heart is liberation, from which (all follows).
If a leaf falls in a ditch, or a river, or a holy place, or a crossroads — what good or bad is that to the tree?

The destruction of body, senses, breath and mind is like the destruction of a leaf, flower or fruit; it is not that of the Self, whose nature is being and bliss, for this does not hold for it as for a tree.
'This is a mass of knowledge' — this indication of the Self, pointing to the truth, is repeated and used to speak of the destruction of the adjunct-bound (self) only.
'Indeed, this Self is imperishable,' says scripture, teaching the imperishability of the Self amid perishing, changing things.

As stones, trees, grass, grain, husks and the like, when burned, become only earth, so the whole visible world — body, senses, breath, mind and the rest — burned by the fire of knowledge, goes to the state of the Supreme Self.
As darkness, being of a different nature, dissolves in the light of the sun, so the whole visible world dissolves in Brahman.
When a pot is destroyed, the space (in it) clearly becomes space; so, on the dissolution of the adjunct, the knower of Brahman himself is Brahman.
As milk poured into milk, oil into oil, water into water becomes one, so the sage who knows the Self (becomes one) in the Self.
Thus, having reached bodiless isolation, undivided being, and the state of Brahman, this ascetic does not return again.
For him whose ignorance and the rest that make up the body have been burned by the knowledge of oneness with the real Self, being Brahman already, how can there be any birth from Brahman?
Bondage and liberation made by Maya do not really exist in one's own Self, as the appearance and disappearance of a snake do not exist in a motionless rope.

Bondage and release would have to be spoken of in terms of the covering, as existent or non-existent; but there is no covering of Brahman, since there is nothing else; if there were, non-duality would be lost, and scripture does not tolerate duality.

The deluded falsely attribute bondage and liberation, qualities of the intellect, to the Reality, like the covering of the eye by a cloud attributed to the sun; for this Imperishable is consciousness, non-dual and unattached.
The notions 'it exists' and 'it does not exist' about the Reality are only qualities of the intellect, not of the eternal Reality.

Therefore bondage and liberation are imagined by Maya and do not belong to the Self. In the Supreme Truth, without parts, actionless, tranquil, blameless, stainless, without a second — how can there be imagination, as of space?
There is no dissolution and no origin, no bound one and no aspirant, no seeker of liberation and no liberated one: this is the ultimate truth.

This supreme, most secret teaching, the essence of the inner conclusion of the crest of all the Vedas (the Upanishads), has been shown to you today by me — to you, who are free of the faults of the Kali age, whose mind is free from desire, and whom I have repeatedly regarded as a seeker of liberation like my own son.
Having thus heard the words of the teacher, bowing with humility, and permitted by him, he went, freed from bondage.
The teacher himself, his mind immersed in the ocean of ever-lasting bliss, roamed the whole earth, purifying it, without interruption.
Thus, through the dialogue of the teacher and the disciple, the nature of the Self has been set forth, for the easy understanding of seekers of liberation.

Let those ascetics who are seekers of liberation, free of all faults of mind that have been prescribed and removed, weary of worldly pleasures, tranquil of mind and fond of the essence of the scriptures, welcome this wholesome teaching.

For those wearied by the burning pain arising from the rays of the sun of affliction on the path of worldly existence, who wander in delusion in a desert seeking water — this speech of Shankara points out to them Brahman, the non-dual, the giver of happiness, the sea of nectar very near at hand; may it be victorious, the bestower of liberation.
